title: The Wheel of the Yugas: A Pilgrimage Against Time
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: L'Enfant de Lyon — The Child by the Rhône

stops.name: Lyon — birthplace, on the thirtieth of September
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of September a daughter is born at Lyon to Maxim Portas, of Greek and Italian blood, and to Julia Nash, an Englishwoman. They name her Maximiani. Three tongues meet in the cradle — Greek, English, French — and she will add many more. From the first she is a solitary, gazing eastward past the confluence of the Rhône and the Saône toward a sun she already loves more than any god of the churches. She will remember herself as a stranger set down in a fallen age, a child of the Golden Age born too late, into the Dark.
suggested_refs: Confluence of the Rhône and Saône at Lyon

stops.name: Lyon — the first cat, the first vow against cruelty
stops.campa: A cat comes into the child's arms, and with it comes the conviction that will run beneath everything she does for seventy years: that the beast is kin, that its pain is real, that to torture it is the great sin of man. Scarcely six years old she refuses meat and turns from the slaughterhouse in horror. She will call this the truest thing she ever felt. Long before Hitler, before India, before the yugas, there is this — a small girl who cannot bear that a living thing should suffer, and who indicts the whole human race for its cruelty.

stops.name: Lyon — the Musée Guimet and the statue of Kali
stops.campa: In the Guimet collection at Lyon the child stands before a bronze Kali, black goddess of destruction and renewal, garlanded with skulls, dancing upon the corpse of time. Something in her answers. Here is a divinity who does not preach meekness or pity for the weak, but the wheel of dissolution and rebirth turning without end. She does not yet have the words for it, but the seed of her whole cosmology is planted before the dancing Mother — creation demands destruction, the Dark Age must be burned away before the Golden can return.

stops.name: Lyon — the station, chalking her defiance in the Great War
stops.campa: At the Lyon railway station, a girl of eleven chalks slogans against the Entente upon the walls. Germany is being crushed and starved, and to her young mind this is an injustice against a noble people; at the same moment Greek refugees are driven from Asia Minor, and she feels their wound as her own. Two loyalties are already fused in her — the Hellenic and the Germanic — and a hatred of what she will later name the leveling, mercantile modern world. The schoolgirl vandal is the priestess in miniature.

segments.name: La Grèce Éternelle — The Making of the Pagan

stops.name: Lyon — the University, chemistry and philosophy
stops.campa: At the University of Lyon the brilliant student takes degrees in science and in philosophy, and toward a doctorate in chemistry writes on the simplicity of nature's mathematical laws. She reads Nietzsche as scripture; on shipboard she devours The Will to Power. In her the exact intellect of the chemist and the ecstatic pagan fuse: she will speak of the Life-Force as a physicist speaks of energy, and worship it as the ancients worshipped the Sun. Rigorous, many-tongued, contemptuous of the herd, she is building the mind that will justify a monstrous faith.

stops.name: Athens — first landfall in the mother-country
stops.campa: On the ninth of August she comes at last to Athens, the mother-country she has claimed since childhood. She reads Nietzsche on the voyage and steps ashore as into a temple. Beneath the Acropolis her pan-Hellenism deepens into something older than nation — a pagan racialism, a mistrust of the Galilean creed that she believes strangled the bright Greek world. She surveys the ruins as living things, not relics. Here the Frenchwoman begins to die and Savitri, servant of the Sun, begins to be born.

stops.name: Delphi — the navel of the world
stops.campa: She walks up to Delphi, to the omphalos where the ancients set the navel of the earth, and stands where the Pythia once breathed the god's madness. The eagle-haunted crags of Parnassus, the sacred way, the fallen columns of Apollo's house — for her these are not archaeology but a religion still smouldering under the ash of twenty Christian centuries. She travels the Peloponnese on foot and on horseback, sleeping in the open, a pilgrim to a faith the world calls dead and she calls the only living truth.

stops.name: Athens — she renounces France, becomes Greek
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of May she signs away her French citizenship and takes the nationality of Greece. It is a religious act more than a legal one: she will belong to the Hellenic world, to the sunlit pagan order, and not to the Republic of the churches and the marketplace. In Athens she completes her studies, a thesis on the reformer-priest Theophilos Kaïris and a degree in chemistry, and she readies herself for a journey east — for she has begun to believe the living Aryan faith survives, not in Europe, but in India.

stops.name: Jerusalem — the pilgrimage that made her a National Socialist
stops.campa: At Eastertide she sails from Athens by way of Rhodes and Cyprus to Palestine. Amid the holy places of the Galilean creed she feels not devotion but revulsion. Here, she decides, is the source of the poison — a slave-morality of pity for the weak, an alien intrusion set against the bright Aryan order of nature and rank. In the very cradle of Christianity, she later declares, she first knew herself to be a National Socialist. The Hellenic pilgrim leaves Palestine having found not her God but her enemy, and her cause.

segments.name: Vers le Soleil — Egypt and the Heretic King

stops.name: Tell el-Amarna — the city of the Sun-Disk
stops.campa: Her heart is captured by Akhnaton, the heretic Pharaoh who three thousand years ago cast down the crowded gods of Egypt and raised one image only — the Aton, the visible Sun, disk of the impersonal Life-Force. At Amarna, the city he built and the desert reclaimed, she reads him as the purest 'Man above Time', the sun-natured seer too gentle for his dark age, undone because he loved life and would not wield the lightning of destruction. She will make him the first pillar of her book, and the measure against which she weighs her own age's avatar.
stops.quote: Akhnaton is, as far as we know, the first person in history to have grasped, and to have tried to bring men back to, the worship of the Life-Force in its highest earthly form: the Sun.
stops.quote_source: A Son of God / Son of the Sun: The Life and Philosophy of Akhnaton (1946)
suggested_refs: Great Temple of the Aten, Amarna

stops.name: Dhanushkodi — landfall in the Holy Land of the East
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of May she steps ashore at Dhanushkodi at the tip of the Indian south, on the day of the full moon of Vaishakha. She has come seeking what she could not find in Europe: an Aryan paganism still breathing, a caste-ordered faith of many gods and no pity for the weak. India, she is certain, is the last unbroken remnant of the primordial Aryan world. She kneels to the land as to a temple regained, and here Maximiani Portas is dissolved: the sun-goddess Savitri claims her at last.

stops.name: Shantiniketan — Tagore, and the name Savitri
stops.campa: At Shantiniketan she meets the poet Rabindranath Tagore, and in Bengal she receives the name that will be hers to the pyre: Savitri, the Sun's own radiance, and Devi, goddess. She learns Bengali and Hindi, adding them to the seven tongues she already commands. She takes formally to Hinduism — not as a convert humbled before a foreign god, but as one who believes she is coming home to the mother-faith of her own Aryan blood, the oldest sunlight, worshipped without shame.

stops.name: Amarnath — the ice-lingam in the Himalaya
stops.campa: She climbs to the cave of Amarnath in the Kashmir heights, where each year an ice-lingam of Shiva rises and melts with the moon — the god of destruction and renewal, the Kali she loved as a child now in his male form, lord of the eternal dance. She keeps her pilgrimages to Gangotri, to the sources of the Ganges, to Mathura at the birth-festival of Krishna. In the wheel of the yugas she reads all history: the Golden Age long fallen, the Kali Yuga at its blackest, and the god who will end it not yet come.

stops.name: Delhi — the Hindu Mission, the wandering lecturer
stops.campa: She enlists in the Hindu Mission and becomes its travelling lecturer, carrying her gospel of Aryan blood and pagan renewal from town to town across the north. She meets Swami Satyananda; she meets Subhas Chandra Bose, whom she reveres as India's warrior-liberator. She teaches too at a college near the capital. To Hindu nationalism she brings the vocabulary of race and purity forged in Europe, and she preaches that India must not be submerged by the alien creeds — a doctrine she will set down as a warning to the whole people.

stops.name: Calcutta — 'A Warning to the Hindus'
stops.campa: At Calcutta the Hindu Mission publishes her Warning to the Hindus, with a preface by the elder Savarkar's brother. In it she proclaims Hindu India the last living fragment of the primordial Aryan spirit, and cries that it must guard its blood and its gods against Islam, against Christianity, against the leveling modern world. It is Europe's racial doctrine dressed in a sari and offered to Bharat as its own. The book makes her a name among the Hindu nationalists — a foreign priestess telling India to be, above all, Aryan.
stops.quote: The Hindus are the last great people on earth to have kept, along with their ancient tongue, the consciousness of the sacredness of blood and soil.
suggested_refs: A Warning to the Hindus, Calcutta 1939

stops.name: Calcutta — marriage to Asit Krishna Mukherji
stops.campa: She weds Asit Krishna Mukherji, a Bengali Brahmin, editor, and open admirer of the Axis. First a civil bond in the autumn of thirty-nine, then on the ninth of June the sacred Hindu rite. Theirs is a marriage of the cause as much as the heart: through his New Mercury and his contacts they gather what serves the Axis, and she will boast that she helped Bose reach the Japanese. To the end she signs herself Savitri Devi Mukherji, keeping the Brahmin name as proof that her blood-faith found, in India, a true and lawful Aryan hearth.

stops.name: Sevagram — the half-hour with Gandhi
stops.campa: At Wardha she is granted half an hour with Gandhi in his ashram at Sevagram. The apostle of non-violence and the priestess of the lightning face each other across an unbridgeable gulf. She cannot abide his ahimsa toward the human world, his pity for the weak, his creed of the spinning-wheel; yet the same woman who scorns his mercy toward men has wept her life long over the suffering of animals. She leaves unmoved, certain that the age of pity must be burned away before the Golden Age can dawn.

stops.name: Varkala — despair on the shore, the war lost
stops.campa: The Reich is in ruins, the god she worshipped in a man is dead in Berlin, and the wheel has turned to its blackest hour. On the beach at Varkala she walks into the sea to end herself. But she does not die. She rises from the water resolved instead upon a mission: to keep the flame, to carry the faith through the long night, to prophesy the one who is still to come — the final avatar, Kalki, who will wield perfect lightning and perfect sun, and shatter the Dark Age at last.

segments.name: L'Homme contre le Temps — The Mythology Takes Shape

stops.name: London — she carries the mission back to Europe
stops.campa: On a British-Indian passport she lands at Southampton and comes up to London, back into the wreck of the West. She lectures on Akhnaton, dances with Ram Gopal's Indian company to earn her bread, and visits her mother in France. But beneath the wandering scholar burns the postwar mission: to reach the defeated Germans, to tell them their faith is not dead but sleeping. She has already begun, from India, the two books that will fix her mythology forever — the indictment of man, and the great tripartite history of Time.

stops.name: London — 'The Impeachment of Man' finished
stops.campa: In the year after the war she completes the strangest of her books — an impeachment of the entire human race for its cruelty to the animals and the earth. Man, she declares, is no lord set above nature but a part of it, and a wicked part; the slaughterhouse, the vivisector's table, the felled forest are his true crimes, beside which he dares to prate of 'war crimes'. The gentleness she withholds from the weak among men she pours out upon the beast — the one strand of her creed the world can almost love, until it sees what it is bound to.

stops.name: Mount Hekla — a night on the burning mountain
stops.campa: Word comes that Hekla, the great volcano of Iceland, has awoken. She hurries north and, on the fourth of April, climbs onto the slopes of the erupting mountain and passes the night amid its fire and thunder. To her this is no natural curiosity but a sacrament — the Life-Force showing its true face, neither good nor evil, creating and destroying in one breath, the lightning and the sun made molten rock. Iceland, land of the old Germanic gods, gives her its burning mountain as a sign that the wheel still turns.

segments.name: Or dans la Fournaise — Germany, the Leaflets, the Prison

stops.name: Occupied Germany — the leaflets from the Nord Express
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of June she boards the Nord Express and rides through the shattered Reich, scattering thousands of handwritten leaflets from the windows and pressing them into hands: Men and women of Germany, hold fast to our glorious National Socialist faith, and resist! She sells her gold jewelry to pay for the printing of bills and posters. Through that summer she slips back in and out, at Saarbrücken and Cologne, pasting her creed upon the walls of the occupied land — a lone missionary of a banned religion in the ruins of its temple.
stops.quote: In distress and defeat, hold fast to our glorious National-Socialist faith and resist!
stops.quote_source: Handwritten leaflet distributed in occupied Germany, 1948 (recounted in Gold in the Furnace)

stops.name: Düsseldorf — the trial
stops.campa: Arrested at Cologne in February for posting her bills, she is brought on the fifth of April before a court at Düsseldorf under the Allied Control Council, charged with spreading National Socialist ideas on German soil. She does not repent; she glories in it, turning the dock into a pulpit. She is sentenced to three years. Far from breaking her, the arrest confirms her sense of destiny: she is the confessor of a persecuted faith, gold thrown into the furnace to be proved, and out of this trial will come her memoir Defiance.

stops.name: Werl — the prison, and the fellowship of the condemned
stops.campa: In the prison at Werl she seeks out her comrades and superiors — the war criminals of the fallen Reich — and finds among the women a friend in a former Belsen wardress. The crypto-Nazi guards indulge her, and she writes in a fever, pouring whole chapters of Gold in the Furnace and The Lightning and the Sun onto paper behind bars. To her the cell is a shrine and captivity an honour. Released in August after some six months, expelled toward India, she carries out the manuscripts that will become her testament.
stops.quote: This whole book was written in the joy of certitude — the certitude that our Ideology is bound to win in the end, whatever be, in the meantime, the fate of those who hold it.

stops.name: Delhi — 'Forever and Ever', the hymns to the Sun
stops.campa: In these years she composes her devotional poems, Forever and Ever — hymns of praise and elegies laid at the feet of the man she calls an avatar, prose-psalms to the Sun and to the vanished order. Here the priestess sings openly what the historian argues in prose: that a god walked among men in her lifetime, was defeated, and will return. The manuscript will be lost for half a century and thought destroyed, surfacing only long after her death, the most nakedly liturgical of all her works.

segments.name: Le Pèlerinage — The Holy Sites of the Reich

stops.name: Braunau am Inn — the birthplace
stops.campa: On the twentieth of April — the birthday of the man she worships — she stands before the house at Braunau am Inn where he was born, and opens her great pilgrimage. Travelling on a Greek passport under her maiden name, she has come by way of Athens, Rome and the Brenner into what she still calls Greater Germany. This is the first station of a via sacra she is inventing as she walks it, treating the wreck of the Third Reich as a landscape of shrines, its dead leader as the fallen sun-god of the age.

stops.name: Berchtesgaden — the ruined Berghof above the Alps
stops.campa: She climbs to Berchtesgaden and the shattered Berghof, the mountain eyrie above the Bavarian Alps, blasted and looted but to her still holy ground. She gathers a splinter, a stone, as another pilgrim gathers relics of a saint. The peaks she reads as an Aryan Olympus, the ruin as a Calvary. Where the tourist sees rubble she sees a temple awaiting its resurrection, and she offers her salute to the empty air where, in her telling, a divine energy once dwelt in mortal form.

stops.name: Munich — the Feldherrnhalle, shrine of the Putsch
stops.campa: In Munich she comes to the Feldherrnhalle, where in 1923 the marchers fell and the movement found its first martyrs. She stands at the cradle-place of the faith as a Christian stands at a martyrium. Nearby lies Landsberg, the fortress where the leader wrote his book in captivity; she goes there too. Each site she binds into her rosary of stations, building in her Pilgrimage a scripture of place, so that later devotees may walk the same road and feel, as she feels, that they tread holy ground.

stops.name: Nuremberg — the empty rally grounds
stops.campa: At Nuremberg she walks the vast, grass-cracked field where once the torch-lit multitudes had roared, now silent under a grey sky, the great tribune stripped of its eagle. To the world it is the scene of judgement, the city of the trials; to her it is a deserted cathedral. She lets the emptiness speak of what was and, in her certainty, what shall be again. The pilgrimage is not mourning only but prophecy: the ruins are seed-ground, and she has appointed herself keeper of the promise of return.

stops.name: Externsteine — the revelation at the Rocks of the Sun
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of October she reaches the Externsteine, the towering sandstone pillars of Westphalia that she takes for the primal Germanic temple of the Sun, where the old cult kept the solstices. She climbs to the high chamber cut to catch the rising light, and there, arm outstretched toward the sun, she receives her revelation: a certainty flooding through her that the Aryan cause is not dead but will rise again, that the wheel will turn back to gold, that victory is written in the very stone. It is the summit of the whole pilgrimage.
stops.quote: I worship impersonal Nature, which is neither 'good' nor 'bad', and who knows neither love nor hatred. I worship Life; the Sun, Sustainer of life.

stops.name: Hermannsdenkmal — the sword against Rome
stops.campa: Close by the Rocks of the Sun she comes to the colossal statue of Hermann, sword lifted to heaven, raised where the Germanic tribes broke three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest nineteen centuries ago. To her the ancient victory and the modern defeat are one story: the northern folk against the leveling empire, the Aryan against the alien. She adds the monument to her stations, and at Emsdetten nearby she lodges with a sympathizer, finishing Pilgrimage and completing, at last, The Lightning and the Sun.

stops.name: Hanover — 'The Lightning and the Sun' completed
stops.campa: On the equinox of the twenty-first of March, at Hanover, she sets down the last words of her magnum opus. In The Lightning and the Sun she weaves the Hindu wheel of the yugas into a single scheme of history: the Man in Time who serves decay, embodied in Genghis Khan the pure destroyer; the Man above Time who resists it in gentleness, Akhnaton of the Sun; and the Man against Time who joins both, wielding the lightning of destruction for the sun's own ends — for which the darkest of dark-age deeds are, in her telling, redeemed. She names the age's avatar and awaits the final one, Kalki.
stops.quote: In this age of gloom, one man stood against Time... the last of those 'lightning-and-sun' men, and the herald of Him Who is to come — Kalki, the Avatar of the end.
suggested_refs: The Lightning and the Sun, Calcutta 1958
Kalki, the tenth avatar of Vishnu

segments.name: Le Fil d'Or — The Wandering Years and Serrano

stops.name: Joda, Orissa — the translator in the iron hills
stops.campa: Expelled from Germany, she returns to India and in the iron-mining country of Orissa takes work as a translator and interpreter to keep herself alive and to pay for the printing of her books. The decades of poverty have begun. She lives sparingly, surrounded by the animals she loves, moving between India and Europe on borrowed passages and the kindness of comrades. The priestess of a dead empire is now a wandering, penniless scholar — yet she holds her certitude undimmed, sure that the golden thread runs unbroken through the black age.
suggested_refs: The Lightning and the Sun, first edition (self-financed)

stops.name: Madrid — with Skorzeny, and the network of comrades
stops.campa: In her wanderings she is drawn into the web of the postwar faithful across the world. At Madrid she stays with Otto Skorzeny; she visits Johann von Leers in Egypt; she begins her long correspondence with Colin Jordan in England. She has become a mother-figure and living relic to the scattered movement, a link between its ruined past and its underground present. The books she wrote in prison and pilgrimage now circulate hand to hand, and a new generation reads her yuga-mythology as revelation.
suggested_refs: Colin Jordan / World Union of National Socialists

stops.name: The Cotswolds — the Cotswold Agreement
stops.campa: In August, in the green hills of the Cotswolds, she is present at the signing of the pact that founds the World Union of National Socialists, and meets the American Rockwell. She is honoured as a matriarch of the cause, the woman who kept the faith through the years of ruin and gave it a sacred history and a scripture of pilgrimage. Yet she remains apart, more mystic than organiser, her eyes on the turning wheel and the avatar to come rather than on the small councils of living men.

stops.name: New Delhi — the last Indian years, alone with the cats
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of June she flies from Paris to Bombay and settles in New Delhi, and here she passes her last long stretch of Indian years — alone but for her cats and, it is said, a cobra she will not have killed. Her husband dies at her side in seventy-seven; her sight fails to cataracts until she can scarcely read; poverty pinches ever harder. Yet she writes and remembers, setting down her Memories and Reflections, an old woman keeping vigil over a creed, faithful to the sun she can no longer clearly see.
suggested_refs: And Time Rolls On / Memories and Reflections

stops.name: New Delhi — the letters to Miguel Serrano
stops.campa: Across the world, in Chile, Miguel Serrano is building his own Esoteric Hitlerism, and the two elders of the same strange faith exchange letters in her last years. She writes to him on the twenty-eighth of March of their loneliness — we are so few in this immense, indifferent world — and of her doctrine of the avatar: that the man she worshipped had too much Sun and not enough Lightning, and that only the last one, Kalki, will hold both in perfect balance and win. Though they never fully read each other, they recognise one another as kin, two keepers of the golden thread.
stops.quote: He had in Him 'too much Sun, not enough Lightning,' because only the last one (the one the Hindu Scriptures call the 'Kalki' avatar) will be equally Sun and Lightning, and will win.
suggested_refs: Savitri Devi's letters to Miguel Serrano

stops.name: New Delhi — the last letter, calling for death the liberator
stops.campa: On the twentieth of April — again the birthday of her god — she writes to Serrano for the last time, half-blind and longing to be gone. Her right eye is already gone, she tells him, and the left is going the same way; every day, she writes, she calls for death, the liberator. She is worn to nothing by age and poverty, yet unrepentant, her creed intact. Within half a year the liberator will come. The final letter closes a correspondence that binds her mythology to Serrano's, the two great voices of Esoteric Hitlerism speaking across the ocean as the light in her fails.
stops.quote: I see almost nothing. My right eye is already kaputt, and now the left is going the same way... Every day I call for death, the liberator!
suggested_refs: Savitri Devi's final letter to Serrano, 1982

segments.name: La Fin et le Feu — Death and the Altar

stops.name: Sible Hedingham — death in an English village
stops.campa: Bound at last for America to speak to her comrades, she breaks her journey in the Essex village of Sible Hedingham, at the house of a friend, and there, shortly after midnight on the twenty-second of October, her heart stops. She is seventy-seven, near-blind, and poor, dying far from Greece and from India in a quiet English lane. Her comrades will say the priestess of the Sun went out with the year's light failing, faithful to the end to the god she served and the avatar she never lived to see.

stops.name: Colchester — the pyre
stops.campa: At Colchester her body is given to the fire, as she wished, in the manner of the faith she took in India — no cross, no priest of the Galilean, only the flame that to her is the Sun's own agent, dissolving the flesh and freeing whatever burns on. The chemist who worshipped Life as energy, the pagan who kept the solstices, returns to the elements she adored. Her ashes are gathered into an inscribed urn and made ready for a long last voyage across the Atlantic.

stops.name: Arlington — the ashes carried to the altar
stops.campa: On the twentieth of February her urn is carried to Arlington in Virginia, to the headquarters of the American movement, and set upon an altar beside the remains of Rockwell in what her followers call a hall of honour. So the priestess who was born by the Rhône, made pagan at Delphi, reborn as a Hindu goddess on the Indian shore, and imprisoned in the ruins of the Reich, comes to rest at last as a relic upon a shrine. In the register of her own creed the wheel has not stopped: she waits there, they say, for the avatar of the end and the return of the gold.
suggested_refs: Urn of Savitri Devi beside Rockwell's remains
